The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

rationales.A: France was not involved in the Pueblo Revolt.
rationales.B: The Pueblos sought to expel the Spanish, not join the English.
rationales.C: The revolt belongs to a wider story: across the Spanish colonies, Native peoples resisted forced labor, tribute, and mission discipline — sometimes by fleeing, sometimes by rebelling. The Pueblo Revolt was the largest and most successful example of that constant resistance, because the mission system demanded the most and suppressed the most. The context is not one uprising but a whole pattern of peoples pushing back against coercion.
rationales.D: No such territorial dispute existed between Spain and Portugal over New Mexico.
rationales.general:
1. Place the revolt in its pattern. Background: across the Spanish colonies, Native peoples resisted forced labor and mission discipline.
2. Ask what made this one the largest. Background: the mission system demanded the most and suppressed the most.
3. Name the context. Not one uprising, but a whole pattern of peoples pushing back against coercion.
Remember: the biggest revolt is usually the loudest example of a quiet, constant pattern.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Colin G. Calloway, New World for All (1997)
stem: In 1680, Pueblo peoples under Popé coordinated an uprising that expelled Spanish colonists and missionaries from New Mexico for over a decade. Which broader development best explains the context of this revolt?

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Colin G. Calloway, New World for All (1997).
stimulus.text: In 1680, Popé, a Tewa religious leader from San Juan, coordinated a rising of the Pueblos that expelled the Spaniards for twelve years; rebels killed friars who had tried to crush their religion and destroyed Catholic ritual objects. When the Spanish returned, they had learned from the experience: where earlier friars had tried to wipe out every Native practice, they now often overlooked them. When Diego de Vargas campaigned to reconquer New Mexico in 1692, Luis, a Picuris leader, greeted him in animal skins with palm-shell headbands — but also wearing a rosary and carrying a silver cross. — paraphrased from Colin G. Calloway, New World for All (1997)
